week.t: NASA History Office: the Gemini XII photograph of the Red Sea and Nile, 14 November 1966, that helped make the case for Landsat
NTU and Canaan announce a four-year, S$7 million collaboration on energy-efficient edge AI
NASA station blog: Menon and Watkins pack Dragon for a Pacific splashdown; still no departure date
Science News Explores: cold-stunned sea-turtle strandings on Cape Cod rose from 139 to 739 a winter
PIB: IIT Jodhpur’s niobium-rich alloy, 7.6 g/cm³, gains 43.48 mg/cm² of oxide at 1,000 °C against 258 for C-103
CERN: construction begins on DUNE’s first cryostat, 17,000 tonnes of liquid argon 1.5 km under South Dakota

tiles.cap: Tomorrow after sunset: point your phone at the sky and flash V-G-R at Voyager 1
tiles.nums: from Wednesday 18 November at 6:16 pm Singapore time, light leaving Earth takes a full day to reach Voyager 1, 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion km) away
tiles.p1: On Tuesday 17 November, after sunset, NASA is asking people everywhere to signal skyward for Voyager 1, in what it calls Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day. NASA’s Voyager site has an “Automated V-G-R Flasher” page: open it on a phone or tablet, point the screen at the sky, and it flashes V-G-R, Voyager’s call sign, in Morse code. Or do it by hand with a torch, bike light or glow stick: V is three quick flashes then one long, G is two long then one quick, R is quick, long, quick. A dot is under a second, a dash about a second, leave a second or more between letters, and keep going for about a minute.
tiles.p2: Why Wednesday: at 5:16:07 am US Eastern on Wednesday 18 November, 6:16 pm in Singapore, Voyager 1 will be 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 km) from Earth, the distance light travels in 24 hours. NASA says it will be the first human-made object to reach that distance.
deep: How far a light-day is

NASA’s page lists the light-times for comparison: the Moon about 1.3 seconds away, the Sun about 8 minutes 20 seconds, Mars 3 to 22 minutes depending on where the two planets are, Neptune four hours and ten minutes, Proxima Centauri about 4.24 light-years. Voyager 1 left Earth on 5 September 1977; NASA’s page gives its speed as nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), though a caption on the same page says around 35,000 mph.
The code

V is · · · —, G is — — ·, R is · — ·. NASA’s timing: a dot under one second, a dash about one second, a brief pause between the symbols of a letter and a second or more between letters, repeated for about a minute. Any light does: torch, glow stick, solar lantern, bike light or phone.
Thursday’s panel

A panel at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Thursday 19 November at 12 pm US Eastern, Friday 20 November at 1 am in Singapore, can be watched online on NASA’s site; participants include Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, and Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager. NASA says a Voyager documentary is planned for 2027, the mission’s 50th anniversary.
The picture
An artist’s concept of a Voyager spacecraft, credit NASA/JPL-Caltech.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Voyager: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day (Stephen Carney) · Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day? (updated 12 Nov 2026) · NASA advisory M26-086, 10 Nov 2026, updated 13 Nov

tiles.cap: Leonids before dawn tomorrow and Wednesday, up to 15 an hour. Mars and Jupiter drift apart
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors under ideal skies in the early hours of 17 and 18 November, after the Moon has set; most people will see fewer
tiles.p1: NASA’s skywatching notes for November put the Leonid meteor shower at its best in the early morning hours of Tuesday 17 and Wednesday 18 November, after the Moon sets: up to about 15 meteors an hour under ideal conditions, fewer for most viewers. Around 12 November the Northern Taurids peaked at a gentler 5 an hour. On the mornings of 15 and 16 November Mars and Jupiter stood about 1.2° apart in the south-east before sunrise; NASA says to keep watching on later mornings as they separate, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish beside it.
tiles.p2: Why now: New Moon was 8 November and first quarter is 17 November; NASA says to look after the Moon sets.
deep: Watch several mornings
NASA suggests watching Mars and Jupiter on more than one morning, to see them close in and then separate again. Jupiter is the brighter of the two.
Three supermoons
The full Moon of 24 November is a supermoon, the first of three in a row: November, December and January. Third quarter follows on 30 November.
Faced the right way

NASA’s chart for 17 November also marks where Voyager 1 sits, in Ophiuchus toward the western horizon at about 5 pm on 17 November, the evening NASA invites people to celebrate Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth.
The photo
NASA’s page opens with the full Moon rising over Vasquez Rocks, north of Los Angeles, photographed by Preston Dyches of NASA on 24 June 2021.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Coming down in Dragon: 3D-printed blood vessels, bacterial DNA, lamps that fake daylight
tiles.nums: of science, supplies and hardware Dragon delivered to the station on 15 October; NASA’s blog still gives no date for its return, only that it is nearing the end of its stay
tiles.p1: NASA’s station blog for Thursday 12 November says the SpaceX Dragon cargo craft is nearing the end of its stay; the crew is loading it for a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, with the last items packed the day before departure. Going down: experiment samples including bacterial DNA and 3D-printed blood vessels, and a set of lighting hardware built to recreate natural daylight and regulate the crew’s sleep, returning after more than three years of testing. Anil Menon and Jessica Watkins began loading payloads; Menon and Joshua Kutryk rearranged cargo to balance its mass and centre of gravity for re-entry.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: the last things in are research samples in portable freezers and incubators, loaded shortly before departure.
deep: Friday’s work

On Friday 13 November Luke Delaney harvested thale cress plants grown in the Multi-use Variable-g Platform in Japan’s Kibo module and preserved samples in the Life Science Glovebox for return to Earth; Menon and Watkins kept packing Dragon; Watkins activated student-designed hardware that tests physical, chemical and biological processes in microgravity.
Spacesuit laundry
Delaney cleaned the cooling and ventilation systems in two spacesuits worn on the 29 October and 5 November spacewalks, which installed roll-out solar arrays on the station.
What NASA has not said

No undocking or splashdown date appears on the blog, which also gives no mission number (NASA’s visiting-vehicles page lists the craft as SpaceX CRS-35, docked 15 October); NASA’s 7 October advisory for the 13 October launch said Dragon would stay until mid-November and splash down off the coast of California. The crew of seven: station commander Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos, Menon, Watkins and Delaney of NASA, and Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency.
The photo
Anil Menon during the 29 October spacewalk, helmet lights on, installing a roll-out solar array on the station’s port truss; photographed by Luke Delaney.
tiles.src: NASA space station blog, 12 Nov 2026: Crew Packs Dragon with Science and Cleans Spacesuits · 13 Nov 2026: Botany, Biomedicine, and Cargo Ops Wrap Up Week Aboard Station

tiles.cap: 241 days, 3,856 orbits: Expedition 74’s crews tell their story. Wednesday, 8 am Singapore
tiles.nums: orbits of Earth by the Soyuz MS-28 crew in 241 days, more than 102 million miles, NASA says
tiles.p1: NASA welcomes the astronauts of Expedition 74 home at Space Center Houston on Tuesday 17 November at 6 pm Central time, which is Wednesday 18 November at 8 am in Singapore; the crew share mission highlights, followed by an awards ceremony. Chris Williams flew with Roscosmos’ Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev on Soyuz MS-28, launched from Baikonur on 27 November 2025 and landed in Kazakhstan on 26 July: 241 days, 3,856 orbits, more than 102 million miles. Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and ESA’s Sophie Adenot flew SpaceX Crew-12, launched 13 February and splashed down off Los Angeles on 8 October: 237 days, more than 3,792 orbits, more than 100 million miles.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: Expedition 74 logged more than 1,400 hours of research, including 3D printing of metal and of tissue, blood-flow research and cancer-related pharmaceutical work.
deep: Who is on stage

NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and Chris Williams; ESA’s Sophie Adenot; Roscosmos’ Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev. Andrey Fedyaev of Roscosmos, who flew on Crew-12, is not available.
Two ways up, two ways down

Soyuz MS-28 went up from Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan and came down on land south-east of Dzhezkazgan, Kazakhstan. Crew-12 went up from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral and came down in the Pacific off Los Angeles.
The photo
The station over the Atlantic, photographed by ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot during the expedition.
tiles.src: NASA Johnson release J26-002, 10 Nov 2026: NASA to Welcome Expedition 74 Astronauts Home at Space Center Houston

tiles.cap: 14 Nov 1966: astronauts photographed the Nile from orbit. Photos like it led to Landsat
tiles.nums: the year Gemini XII flew, 11 to 15 November, the last mission of NASA’s Gemini programme, and the year the satellite programme that became Landsat was conceived
tiles.p1: On 14 November 1966, James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr., orbiting Earth on Gemini XII, photographed the Red Sea and the Nile valley below them. NASA’s History Office published the frame on Friday 13 November, 60 years almost to the day after it was taken. Gemini XII, 11 to 15 November 1966, was the final mission of the Gemini programme, flown to work out the rendezvous and spacewalk procedures the Moon missions would need; the photographs that Lovell, Aldrin and other Gemini astronauts brought back also demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for looking closely at Earth’s surface.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: William T. Pecora, director of the US Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971, said in 1969 that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite programme was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility” of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography for Earth-resource work. That programme led to Landsat.
deep: From snapshot to satellite

NASA calls Pecora one of the strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites. Over more than five decades, NASA says, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided data used for monitoring crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health and land use.
The line continues

NASA Earth Observatory’s image of 13 November set a Landsat 5 view of mangroves in Burma from 14 February 2010 beside a Landsat 9 view from 2 February 2026, part of a record stretching back to 1984 that shows mangroves lost nearly 3,000 square kilometres worldwide between 1984 and 2010 and regained nearly 2,000 after 2010, in a record of imagery running to 2023.
The photo
NASA’s photograph of the Red Sea and the Nile valley area, taken by Lovell and Aldrin on 14 November 1966 during the four-day Gemini XII mission.
tiles.src: NASA History Office, 13 Nov 2026: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program · NASA Earth Observatory, 13 Nov 2026: A Global Rebound for Mangroves

tiles.cap: IIT Jodhpur’s alloy for 1,000 °C: 7.6 g/cm³, growing about a sixth of the oxide C-103 does
tiles.nums: of oxide gained after 24 hours at 1,000 °C, against 258 mg/cm² for the conventional alloy C-103, the Press Information Bureau reports
tiles.p1: Materials engineers at IIT Jodhpur have made a niobium-rich alloy they call a Refractory Complex Lean Alloy, the Press Information Bureau reported on Tuesday 10 November. Its density is about 7.6 g/cm³, where conventional refractory high-entropy alloys are typically above 10 to 12 g/cm³ and the established alloys C-103 and WC3009 sit at about 9 to 10. After 24 hours at 1,000 °C it gained 43.48 mg/cm² of oxide against 258 mg/cm² for C-103; at room temperature it has a yield strength of 1.13 GPa and takes a compressive strain of about 29%.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: the alloy leaves out hafnium, one of the rarest and most expensive ingredients of alloys like C-103, for an estimated cost advantage of about 11 times; IIT Jodhpur names hypersonic and re-entry vehicles, rocket propulsion and defence platforms as potential future uses, after more testing.
deep: Who

Dr Saurabh Nene, Associate Professor in the Department of Materials Engineering, led the work with postdoctoral fellows Dr Dharmendra Yadav and Dr Akshit Dutta and PhD scholar Aditya Balpande; it is published in Materials & Design. “The central idea behind this research was to rethink how high-temperature refractory alloys are designed,” Nene said.
The trade-off

“Conventional materials often involve a trade-off between weight, mechanical formability and oxidation resistance,” said Nene. The team says its Complex Lean Alloy approach brings those properties together, that the work was carried out indigenously at IIT Jodhpur, and that defect-free samples of 20 to 200 g were made in-house.
What happens at 1,000 °C

Hot metal in air grows a skin of oxide, and the mass it gains is a measure of how much has formed: 43.48 against 258 mg/cm² is roughly a sixfold difference. Next come tests of strength, creep and fatigue at high temperature, and scaling up.
tiles.src: Press Information Bureau (PIB Jaipur), Ministry of Education, 10 Nov 2026, release 2334624: IIT Jodhpur Develops Next-Generation Lightweight Refractory Alloy with Exceptional Oxidation Resistance at 1,000°C · Materials & Design

tiles.cap: NTU and Canaan put S$7 million into AI that runs on less power, out at the edge
tiles.nums: over four years for the NTU–Canaan Green Intelligent Compute Collaboration, announced Friday 13 November: four PhD researchers, about 10 papers, four technical reports and working prototypes
tiles.p1: AI is moving out of giant data centres and into shops, cameras and devices at the “edge”, and every one of them uses electricity. In a release on Friday 13 November, NTU and Canaan said they have launched a four-year, S$7 million collaboration, hosted at NTU’s Centre in Computational Technologies for Finance, to design energy-aware computing, privacy-preserving edge AI for smart retail, inference shared between cloud, edge and end devices, and new edge-AI training modules. It is to produce four PhD researchers, about 10 academic papers, four technical work-package reports, industrial prototypes and patents where commercially applicable.
tiles.p2: Why here: NTU ties the work to Singapore’s updated National AI Strategy (2026), its Green Data Centre Roadmap and the Singapore Standard SS 715:2025.
deep: The problem

“As AI moves beyond centralised data centres and into more diverse real-world environments, computing efficiency is becoming a system-level challenge - spanning chips, software, workload scheduling and energy use,” said Nangeng Zhang, Canaan’s founder, chairman and CEO.
NTU’s view

“As artificial intelligence expands across every sector, managing its environmental footprint has become a critical global challenge,” said Professor Shirley Meng, NTU’s Vice President (Industry). The agreement was first signed on 7 May 2026; the research team is led by Associate Professor Tianwei Zhang, Associate Director of the centre and Provost’s Chair in computing.
The photo
Representatives from NTU and Canaan at the launch, among them Nangeng Zhang, Professor Shirley Meng and Professor Wen Yonggang, NTU’s Vice Provost (Graduate Education) and Director of the centre.
tiles.src: NTU News, 13 Nov 2026: S$7 million NTU-Canaan partnership to drive advances in sustainable computing and edge AI · NTU CCTF news, 7 May 2026

tiles.cap: NTU glue cured from inside by magnetic nanoparticles. One hour matched 24 hours in an oven
tiles.nums: adhesive coatings cured by magnetic induction for one hour reached bonding strength comparable to coatings baked in a conventional oven for 24 hours, NTU reports
tiles.p1: Paints, glues and resins on car and aircraft parts are usually cured by putting the whole component into an industrial oven. NTU’s alternative, called Spinheat, mixes specially designed magnetic nanoparticles into the coating; an alternating magnetic field makes the particles generate heat inside the material, so the coating cures from within and heat-sensitive parts are spared. On Thursday 12 November NTU announced a partnership with Motherson, a design, engineering and manufacturing company with more than 475 facilities in 47 countries, to take it towards the factory floor.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: in the lab, one hour under the magnetic field matched 24 hours in an oven, and NTU says it could cut energy use, carbon emissions and the space taken up by curing equipment.
deep: Who and how

Professor Raju V. Ramanujan and Associate Professor Terry Steele of NTU’s School of Materials Science and Engineering lead the work; NTU first demonstrated magnetic-field-activated epoxy curing in 2020. The latest version reads the temperature in real time and adjusts the field, delivering heat only when needed, to reduce overheating, bubbles and other defects.
Next

“The next challenge is to understand how this can work reliably within automotive manufacturing,” said Steele. The work is funded by the National Research Foundation under its 29th Competitive Research Programme, was published in Applied Materials Today earlier in 2026, and the intellectual property is filed through NTUitive.
The partner
Motherson makes automotive and aerospace components; Dhruv Mehra, Director of Motherson Singapore, is quoted for the company in the announcement.
tiles.src: NTU News, 12 Nov 2026: NTU, Motherson to develop magnetic technology to cut manufacturing time and energy use

tiles.cap: A metre stick with a lump of clay near one end is easier to balance on a finger clay-up
tiles.nums: from one end of a 1 m dowel, the Exploratorium puts a fist-sized lump of clay; balance it on a fingertip clay-down, then clay-up, and the second is easier
tiles.p1: Take a wooden dowel about 1 m long and 1.25 cm thick and press a fist-sized lump of clay around it about 20 cm from one end. Balance it upright on the tip of your finger with the clay end down, near your hand. Then flip it so the clay is at the top. The Exploratorium’s Balancing Stick snack asks which is easier; the answer is that with the heavy end up, the stick is easier to keep balanced.
tiles.p2: Why: with the mass far from your hand the stick has more rotational inertia, so it starts to tip more slowly and you have more time to adjust and keep it balanced; with the mass low it has less rotational inertia and tips faster.
deep: Inertia of turning

Rotational inertia depends not only on how much mass there is but on how far it sits from the axis the object turns about, here your fingertip. The same clay, moved from near your hand to near the far end of the 1 m stick, makes the stick far more reluctant to rotate, though its mass has not changed.
Feel it

Hold the stick by the end near the clay, then by the far end, and swing it as if casting a fishing line: it is much harder to move fast with the clay far from your hand than with the clay near it, the Exploratorium notes, with the same mass in both cases.
The contest

The Exploratorium’s challenge for a group: hand out the clay and dowel separately, let each person fix the clay wherever they like with the dowel sticking out at both ends, and see who balances longest. Let the group discover the clay’s role for themselves.

tiles.cap: 17,000 t of argon at −185 °C, 1.5 km down, waiting for neutrinos fired from 1,300 km away
tiles.nums: from Fermilab in Batavia, Illinois, to the DUNE far detectors at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota
tiles.p1: Nearly 1.5 km underground in South Dakota, crews from Fermilab, CERN and the Sanford Underground Research Facility have begun building the first of two giant cryostats for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, CERN reported on Tuesday 10 November. Each is an insulated container 66 m long, 19 m wide and 18 m high that will hold about 17,000 tonnes of liquid argon at about −185 °C. Its frame uses 2,600 red steel beams, part of more than 6,200 tonnes of steel contributed by CERN and carried one by one from the surface down to the assembly area. From 2031 a neutrino beam from Fermilab, 1,300 km away, is expected to reach it.
tiles.p2: Why: neutrinos may explain why the Universe ended up mostly matter; the detector will also watch particles arriving from the Sun and from deep space.
deep: Timeline

Assembly of the second cryostat starts in 2027 in the North Cavern; the underground spaces are completed in 2029, the detector in 2030, and the beam arrives in 2031. The experiment is slated to run until the late 2040s. More than 1,500 researchers are in the collaboration today, 1,800 from 2030.
Who said what

“DUNE is Fermilab’s top priority,” said Norbert Holtkamp, the director of Fermilab. “SURF is proud to support this world-class research 1478 metres below ground level,” said Mike Headley, the lab’s director. “This brings us one step closer to science,” said Jolie Macier, project manager for the far detectors and cryogenics.
CERN’s part

“Collaboration is in CERN’s DNA, and our contribution to DUNE is a brilliant example of cross-organisational partnership,” said Mark Thomson, CERN’s Director-General. The steel came from CERN as an in-kind contribution; Lluís Miralles, principal project engineer of CERN’s Neutrino Platform, is quoted on the build.
The picture
Construction of the first cryostat began in early November, photographed by Matthew Kapust of SURF.
tiles.src: CERN, 10 Nov 2026: Construction begins on massive underground neutrino experiment designed to unlock the secrets of the Universe
tiles.credit: Photo: Matthew Kapust, SURF, via CERN

tiles.cap: ASUS’s Zenbook Duo: two 14-inch OLED screens, 1.65 kg. The keyboard is a Bluetooth lid
tiles.nums: dual-battery system in a laptop that carries two 14-inch 3K OLED touchscreens; 1.35 kg without the detachable keyboard, 1.65 kg with it
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes the ASUS Zenbook Duo (model UX8407AA). It looks like an ordinary 14-inch touchscreen laptop until you lift the keyboard: it is a Bluetooth keyboard held on by magnets, and under it is a second 14-inch 3K (2880 × 1800) OLED touchscreen, 144 Hz, 500 nits typical and 1,000 nits peak in HDR. A kickstand and a hinge that folds flat let the two screens stand side by side or one above the other. Inside: an Intel Core Ultra Series 3 chip (up to the Core Ultra X9 388H, 16 cores, up to 5.1 GHz), 16 or 32 GB of memory soldered on, a 99 Wh battery, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI 2.1 and Wi-Fi 7, in a chassis ASUS calls Ceraluminum, 1.96 cm thick with the keyboard, 1.65 kg.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: Tom’s Guide’s Jason England, who gave it an Editor’s Choice, still wrote “It’s just a shame about that price,” from $2,099, $2,299 as reviewed; he measured 435.2 nits and 87.2% of the DCI-P3 colour range, below the 500 nits and 100% DCI-P3 on ASUS’s spec sheet, and found that for graphics “AMD is still ahead.”
deep: The seesaw

ASUS product manager Nin Chiang told TIME that the hard part was making the combined display usable both vertically and horizontally; the answer was balancing the weight of the components on each side so the device balances “like a seesaw.”
Docking

ASUS’s MagLatch docking uses retractable pogo pins to connect the keyboard when it sits on the lower screen; its ScreenXpert software notices when the lid opens beyond 175°. Six speakers, 1.7 mm of key travel, and, per ASUS’s spec page, a stylus and a wireless mouse in the box.
Numbers that disagree

ASUS’s spec table says 500 nits typical and 100% DCI-P3; Tom’s Guide measured 435.2 nits and 87.2%. ASUS’s spec table gives no battery-life figure; the reviewer got up to 14 hours in testing and 2 h 12 min in a gaming test. The review page carries several prices: from $2,099, $2,299 as reviewed, and retailer listings of $2,399.99 and $2,699.99.
Praise

“The two OLED displays here are simply mesmerizing,” England wrote, and “Price aside, this is a belter.” He found the hinge “folds back on itself and stows away to make the fully extended form a fully flat panel,” and the speakers the most surprising upgrade.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Martin Cizmar): ASUS Zenbook Duo · ASUS Zenbook Duo UX8407 tech specs and press release · Tom’s Guide review (Jason England, 26 Jan 2026)

tiles.cap: A $59 concrete-grey puck with no battery. Tap your phone on it, or your apps stay locked
tiles.nums: Brick has no battery, no charger and no Wi-Fi: an NFC chip in a magnetic puck is the physical key that unlocks the apps you have blocked
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes Brick, built by TJ Driver, then 23, and his college friend Zach Nasgowitz: an app that blocks whatever apps you choose, and a small concrete-coloured puck with an NFC chip inside. To unlock the blocked apps you have to walk to the puck and physically tap your phone on it. Driver’s reason: his phone “was getting in the way.” The puck needs no battery, no charging and no Wi-Fi; it has a magnet and an anti-slip silicone base, and one puck works with any number of phones. Android 12 or iOS 17 and up; $59.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: Tom’s Guide’s Ashley Thieme says it “relies on human traits of laziness”, that with five emergency unbricks on hand, being able to turn blocks off in the app “doesn’t create that much of a barrier”, and that it is not going to “win any design awards”. Also: “If you don’t have the willpower to wait it out, this may not be for you.”
deep: The engineering

Tom’s Guide notes the chip is NFC, not RFID, so the phone has to be held close; the puck measures 2 × 2 inches and weighs 3.17 ounces. TIME’s line: often the tap is “all the friction needed to get you to do something other than doomscroll.”
Modes and escape hatches
Up to 10 custom modes; a remote lock by holding the virtual Brick in the app for 5 seconds; five Emergency Unbricks included, each of which unblocks everything without the puck. No recurring fees.
The numbers do not all agree

Brick’s product page says iOS 17.0 or later; its FAQ says iOS 18.0 or later. The company quotes a survey of more than 3,500 users in which over 95% felt less distracted; that is the maker’s own survey.
Praise
Tom’s Guide gave it an Editor’s Choice badge: “The Brick offers the best way to curb excessive phone usage,” and “effective at reducing screen time and social media usage.” A rival, Bloom, costs $39.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Daniel Varghese): Brick · getbrick.com product page and FAQ · Tom’s Guide review (Ashley Thieme, 2 Oct 2026)

tiles.cap: A metre of string across your ears: pluck it and you hear a note nobody else can
tiles.nums: the pitch of a string rises with the square root of its tension, and rises as the string gets shorter; the sound is so quiet that nobody close to you is disturbed
tiles.p1: Take a piece of string at least 1 m long. Put the middle behind your head, bring the two halves forward across your ears so the string crosses each ear opening, and hold the loose ends together in front of your face. Pluck. You hear your string, but so quietly that, the Exploratorium says, you will not disturb other people even if they are close to you. Pull tighter: the note goes up. Slide your hand along to shorten the string while keeping the pull the same: higher again.
tiles.p2: The rule, from the Exploratorium: frequency is proportional to the square root of the tension and inversely proportional to the length; higher frequency is a higher note.
deep: Two knobs

Tension and length are the two things you can change. Double the tension and the frequency rises by √2, about 1.41 times; halve the length at the same tension and it doubles. Try to hear the difference between the two moves.
Why only you
The Exploratorium does not say why the sound stays with you; ask a friend to stand a hand’s width away and report what they hear, then swap places.
The Exploratorium’s joke
“Many city bus services do not allow people to play loud music on buses,” the Exploratorium notes; a head harp keeps you within the rules, and you get “more room as others move away from you.”

tiles.cap: MIT’s phrase for what a chatbot answer can create: “the illusion of learning”
tiles.nums: principles in MIT’s 2026 report on AI in education
tiles.p1: MIT’s report does not call for banning AI. One of its eight principles is augmentation, not automation: AI should be used to “augment and enhance curiosity, creativity, and learning, not automate them.” Its named risks are the ones you would expect, weaker memory and confidence, falling back on AI at the first hint of struggle, and one you might not: fewer people. MIT saw fewer students at office hours and, anecdotally, fewer in-person groups in dorms and libraries, turning to AI instead of to classmates, TAs or professors.
tiles.p2: The point: the product of school is you, not the mark.
deep: What MIT asks of its own students
Learn to write good prompts, check every output, recognise when it has made something up, and know when not to use it at all.
Why checking matters

The report warns that models hallucinate, so students need to learn when an output is likely to be made up. MIT’s guidance for research: a human is responsible for verifying the output, and AI should never be listed as a co-author.
Keep it human

The report says every subject should include a regular in-person social component, calls for more project-based work, and asks for deliberately AI-free experiences and AI-free spaces for interaction and assessment.
tiles.src: MIT Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training, Aug 2026

tiles.cap: Below 10 °C a sea turtle gets too cold to swim. Cape Cod rescues: 139 a winter, then 739
tiles.nums: cold-stunned sea turtles stranded on Cape Cod beaches per winter: the average for 1999–2003, then for 2019–2023, Science News Explores reports
tiles.p1: Sea turtles do best in water of about 17 to 29 °C; below 10 °C they are “cold-stunned”, too chilled to swim or eat, and drift onto beaches. On Cape Cod, Massachusetts, strandings averaged 139 a winter in 1999 to 2003 and 739 in 2019 to 2023. Warmer seas lead the turtles, many of them young Kemp’s ridleys, north into risky waters; when autumn cold arrives, conditions “change very rapidly, too fast for them to figure out how to escape,” says biologist Samir Patel. Volunteers patrol the beaches around high tide, when turtles are most likely to wash ashore, and the New England Aquarium’s sea-turtle hospital warms the survivors by about 2.8 °C a day.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: “All of these turtles really should be dead after being out at sea in extreme cold and not eating,” says Adam Kennedy, who directs the hospital, yet about three-quarters of the rescued Massachusetts turtles in recent years healed and were released.
deep: Slowly
The safe warming rate is about 2.8 °C (5 °F) a day. One loggerhead, patient number 671, arrived with a body temperature of 8.2 °C and left six months later at 42 kg, having gained 10.7 kg.
The West Coast too

On the Pacific coast, 68 cold-stunned turtles were documented between 2009 and 2024, from Santa Barbara, California, to British Columbia, and as many as 70% of them die. Veterinarian Heather Harris: “The turtles they see on the East Coast are predominantly immature Kemp’s ridleys.”
Why every one counts

Sea turtles take 10 to 50 years to mature and females lay only every two to four years, so “for species recovering from near-extinction, every animal matters,” says Harris. On 23 June more than 100 people watched 12 rehabilitated turtles go back into the sea. “We never count a turtle out,” says Kennedy.

tiles.cap: Corner of your eye: how close must a shape come before you can read the word on it?
tiles.nums: steps marked along a table edge from 0° straight ahead to 90° at each side, so you can record the angle at which motion, colour, shape and letters first appear
tiles.p1: Hold both fists out at eye level. Your partner tapes a dot on your left thumbnail, over the 0° mark, and a hidden paper shape, a bit over 2.5 cm across with a coloured shape and a three- or four-letter word on it, on your right thumb, held out past 90°. Stare at the dot and slowly swing your right arm in an arc toward it. Without moving your eyes, say when you first detect motion, then colour, then shape, then the word. The Exploratorium’s Peripheral Vision snack marks a table edge every 10° with tape so your partner can record each angle. Expect the shape to get surprisingly close to the dot before the details arrive.
tiles.p2: Why: the colour-sensing cones crowd the centre of the retina and thin out toward its edge, so something seen from the corner of the eye loses its colour; rods are spread more evenly but also thin out, which limits shape; the fovea, the small dense centre, covers only a couple of square millimetres.
deep: Set-up

A partner, a protractor, about 1 m of string, tape and a table at least 1.3 m wide. Sit centred on the long side, mark a 0° point about two-thirds of a metre in front of you at the far edge, and use arm, string and protractor to tape marks every 10° out to 90° on each side. Draw shapes a little over 2.5 cm wide, each with a 3- or 4-letter word (DOG, CAT, EYE) the person being tested has not seen.
Movement wins

Peripheral vision is very sensitive to motion, probably an evolutionary advantage, the Exploratorium notes. Generally you are not aware of how little you see off-centre, the Exploratorium says, because your eyes are always in motion.
Keep your eyes still
As the coloured shape nears the middle it becomes hard not to glance at it; a second person should watch the eyes and stop the trial if they move. Switch arms and partners for more data.
